Tonbridge.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of West Kent
s1loc: Tonbridge anchors a busy West Kent visitor economy around Tonbridge Castle, the finest motte-and-bailey in the county, whose 13th-century gatehouse, armoury and tower views over the River Medway draw day-trippers all year. Just beyond the town, Penshurst Place and Gardens and Hever Castle, the childhood home of Anne Boleyn, pull heritage crowds, while the Big Cat Sanctuary at Smarden and Knole House at nearby Sevenoaks widen the marquee draw across the Medway valley.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the river and out into the countryside, led by the 160-acre Haysden Country Park with its freshwater lakes, sailing, boating and fishing, waymarked trails and natural play area. Tonbridge River Trips cruise the Medway aboard the electric Enid May, the Tonbridge Sportsground offers a skate park and crazy golf, and the Big Cat Sanctuary and surrounding High Weald keep activity operators working through the warm season.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the medieval market core and the restored Hadlow Tower folly in the Medway valley to the Tonbridge Castle Music Weekend each July, when Proms-style concerts fill the castle grounds. The Oast Theatre, local vineyards and the events calendar at the castle lawns add cultural weight, with the historic high street, the old town quarter and the riverside walk tying the heritage offer together.

Underpinning it all is a hotel base led by the Premier Inn Tonbridge North and country guest houses across the Weald, plus a tour-operator and guide scene built around the castle, Penshurst and Hever. Tonbridge railway station sits on the mainline to London Charing Cross, London Bridge and Cannon Street in around 40 minutes, and the A21 and M26 corridor put Sevenoaks, Knole and the wider Kent countryside within an easy day trip.

Rushden.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of North Northamptonshire
s1loc: Rushden anchors a growing North Northamptonshire visitor economy around Rushden Lakes, a 30-acre shopping and leisure destination set against 214 acres of lakes in the Nene Valley, with a 12-screen Cineworld and stores including Marks and Spencer, House of Fraser, Primark and H and M. The waterside boardwalks, the RSPB Nene Wetlands visitor centre and the nature reserve draw shoppers and walkers off the A45 across the whole year.

The leisure and activity layer spreads out from the lakeside, led by Paradise Island Adventure Golf and the Flip Out trampoline park for families, with Stanwick Lakes country park and its visitor centre, splash play and waterside trails just to the north. Skylark Studios, the Nene Valley watersports and the wider Nene Wetlands give activity operators a busy seasonal base, and Hall Park gives the town its own 32 acres of riverside green space.

Heritage and culture run through Rushden Museum in Hall Park, which tells the story of the town's boot, shoe and lace-making powerhouse era, and Rushden Hall, the 14th-century manor that is the town's oldest domestic building. The Rushden Transport Museum and Railway in the Victorian station, the medieval St Mary's Church and the 17-point town heritage trail keep a cultural calendar turning through the year.

Underpinning it all is a roadside and town hotel base around the A45 and Rushden Lakes, with a tour-operator and guide scene built around the lakes and the Nene Valley. Wellingborough railway station links the town to London St Pancras and the Midland mainline, the A6 and A45 corridor put Kettering, Bedford and the Nene country within an easy day trip, and Stanwick Lakes feeds a steady seasonal flow of visitors into the area.

Pontefract.region: Pontefract and the Five Towns of West Yorkshire
Pontefract.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Five Towns
s1loc: Pontefract anchors a busy West Yorkshire visitor economy around Pontefract Castle, the once-mighty stronghold known as Pomfret Castle in Shakespeare and reputed scene of the death of Richard II, whose free-to-enter grounds, visitor centre and Proms at the Castle concerts draw crowds across the year. Pontefract Racecourse, one of the longest continuous circuits in Europe, brings a packed calendar of race days and the small Pontefract Races Museum into the old market town.

The leisure and activity layer spreads through Valley Gardens, the town's floral park with play areas and sports space, and out to the reclaimed countryside of the Five Towns. The nearby Xscape Yorkshire complex at Castleford, with its Snozone real-snow slope and climbing walls, RSPB Fairburn Ings and the Aire and Calder Navigation towpath give activity and watersports operators a busy seasonal base around the M62 corridor.

Heritage and culture run through Pontefract Museum, housed in a magnificent art nouveau building in the old Carnegie Library, which tells the story of the town's liquorice and glass industries. The legendary Pontefract Cakes and the Pontefract Liquorice Festival celebrate the town's confectionery roots, while the medieval St Giles' Church, the Buttercross and the bustling market keep a cultural calendar turning across the Five Towns.

Underpinning it all is a town and roadside hotel base, including Rogerthorpe Manor, and a guide scene built around the castle, racecourse and liquorice heritage. Pontefract has three railway stations - Monkhill, Tanshelf and Baghill - linking Leeds, Wakefield, Doncaster and York, and the A1 and M62 corridor put Castleford, Featherstone and the wider region within an easy day trip and a steady seasonal flow.

Camberley.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Surrey Heath
s1loc: Camberley anchors a Surrey Heath visitor economy shaped by the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, the historic officer-training college founded in 1812, whose Old College, Royal Memorial Chapel and Grand Entrance open to visitors on scheduled tours and open days. The town grew up alongside the academy, and the military draw, the Camberley Theatre and the surrounding heathland give the area a distinctive year-round pull off the M3 corridor.

The leisure and activity layer is built on green space, led by Frimley Lodge Park, a Green Flag site on the Basingstoke Canal with a miniature railway, pitch and putt, sports pitches and play areas, and the 59-hectare Lightwater Country Park of heathland, ponds and woodland. The Lookout Discovery Centre near Bracknell, with its interactive science exhibits and treetop walkway through Swinley Forest, adds a busy family activity draw close by.

Heritage and culture run through the Surrey Heath Museum, with displays on local history and the military, and the Sandhurst collection of uniforms and artefacts from the Royal Military Academy. High Cross Church on Knoll Road serves as a community arts and events venue at the town centre, while the Camberley Theatre and the 18th-century Obelisk folly on the ridge widen the heritage and cultural offer across the borough.

Underpinning it all is a hotel base around the M3 and the town centre, with a tour-operator and guide scene built around Sandhurst and the heathland country parks. Camberley sits close to the South West Main Line, the A30 and the M3, with Farnborough, Bracknell and the wider Surrey and Berkshire borders within an easy day trip, and the heaths and forests feeding a steady seasonal flow of walkers and cyclists.

Kendal.region: Kendal and the south of the Lake District
Kendal.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Lakeland gateway
s1loc: Kendal, the Auld Grey Town built from local limestone, is the southern gateway to the Lake District and a marquee draw in its own right. Kendal Castle, the ruined 12th-century home of the Parr family above the River Kent, gives sweeping views over the town, while Abbot Hall beside the river, the Kendal Museum and the famous Kendal Mint Cake carried by Hillary and Tenzing on Everest in 1953 pull a steady stream of Lakeland visitors.

The leisure and activity layer runs straight into the fells, with Scout Scar and the Kent valley giving walkers and cyclists open country on the town's edge. Sizergh Castle and its 1,600-acre National Trust estate of woodland, wetland and gardens, and Levens Hall with the oldest topiary gardens in the world, sit just south of town, while the River Kent and the surrounding Lakeland trails keep outdoor operators busy across the warm season.

Heritage and culture run through the Brewery Arts Centre, a year-round complex of theatre, music, film and craft workshops, and the historic yards and ginnels that thread off Kendal's main streets. The Kendal Museum's natural history and archaeology collections, the medieval Holy Trinity Church and the town's calendar of festivals, including the famous Kendal Mountain Festival, keep a strong cultural offer turning through the year.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel and guest-house base serving Lake District visitors, with a tour-operator and guide scene built around the fells and the National Trust estates. Kendal sits on the Windermere branch line off the West Coast Main Line at Oxenholme, with the M6 close by, putting Lancaster, Penrith, Windermere and the southern Lakes within an easy day trip and a strong seasonal draw.

Ruislip.region: Ruislip and the London Borough of Hillingdon
Ruislip.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north-west London
s1loc: Ruislip anchors a north-west London visitor economy around Ruislip Lido, a former reservoir set within Ruislip Woods, London's first National Nature Reserve, with a sandy beach, a miniature railway and waterside walks that draw families across the year. The Manor Farm heritage site at the north end of the High Street, with its motte-and-bailey remains and Tudor buildings, gives the area a thousand years of history and a free, walkable visitor core.

The leisure and activity layer runs through the 726 acres of Ruislip Woods - Park Wood, Mad Bess Wood, Copse Wood and Bayhurst Wood - laced with trails, plus the Ruislip Lido Railway that carries visitors round the water on a narrow-gauge line. The River Pinn, the duck pond markets at Manor Farm and the surrounding Hillingdon parks and golf courses keep family and outdoor operators busy through the warm season.

Heritage and culture centre on Manor Farm, Hillingdon's flagship heritage site, where the Grade II* Great Barn built from Ruislip Woods timber around 1300 is among the oldest timber-framed buildings in Greater London. The Tudor Manor Farm House visitor centre, the 16th-century Little Barn library, the craft cart sheds and the medieval St Martin's Church anchor a year-round programme of markets, fairs and events.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house base across Hillingdon, with a guide scene built around Manor Farm and the Lido. Ruislip sits on the Metropolitan and Piccadilly lines and the Chiltern route, with the A40 close by, putting Uxbridge, Harrow, central London and Heathrow within an easy day trip, and the woods and Lido feeding a steady seasonal flow of day visitors into the area.

Malvern.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Malvern Hills
s1loc: Great Malvern anchors a Worcestershire visitor economy built around the Malvern Hills, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty of 680-million-year-old rock whose Worcestershire Beacon gives 360-degree views into Wales. The town has been a tourism destination since the Victorian Water Cure, when Malvern Water from the hills drew Florence Nightingale, Charles Dickens and Charles Darwin, and visitors still sample the springs at the Malvina fountain in the town centre.

The leisure and activity layer runs straight onto the hills, with walking, cycling and the network of springs, spouts and wells threading up the ridge from St Ann's Well to the Beacon. The surrounding commons, the wooded slopes and the trails of the Malvern Hills Trust give outdoor operators a busy seasonal base, while the Morgan Experience Centre at the Morgan Motor Company workshop draws visitors to watch its hand-built sports cars come together.

Heritage and culture run through Malvern Theatres, opened in 1885 as the Winter Gardens and long associated with George Bernard Shaw and Sir Edward Elgar, and Great Malvern Priory, a former Benedictine monastery with some of the oldest medieval stained glass in the country. The Malvern Museum in the medieval Abbey Gateway, the Three Counties Showground hosting the RHS Malvern Spring Festival and Royal Three Counties Show, and the Well Dressing festival keep a full calendar turning.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house base shaped by the spa era, with a tour-operator and guide scene built around the hills, the priory and the showground. Great Malvern railway station, in its restored Victorian buildings, links Worcester, Hereford and Birmingham, and the surrounding Three Counties countryside puts Worcester, Hereford and the Wye valley within an easy day trip and a strong seasonal draw.
